blocks.text: Define a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, and let the caller choose one at runtime.

A **context** holds a **strategy** and delegates one varying decision to it. The context never learns which concrete strategy it has, so a new algorithm means a new class or lambda, not an edit to the context.

items: **Varies:** one algorithm or policy (pricing, sorting, retry, compression).
**Stays stable:** the code that uses it.
**Chosen by:** the client or configuration, usually once per use.

blocks.text: In Java 8+ a one-method strategy is a functional interface, so a lambda or method reference is a complete strategy.

walkthrough.note: The strategy interface: one method. `@FunctionalInterface` lets lambdas implement it and makes the compiler enforce that.
Concrete strategies as records: immutable, validated in the compact constructor, each knowing only its own rule.
The context takes a strategy in its constructor and delegates the one varying step. No `switch`, no `instanceof`.
A lambda is a full strategy. Trivial rules need no class at all.
Selection lives at the edge, in a map from promo code to policy. A new promo touches this map, never `Checkout`.
The client pairs context with strategy and calls the context. The same `Checkout` prints three different totals.

blocks.text: Shipping quotes in an online shop.

Each carrier prices parcels differently: weight tables, zones, surcharges. The customer picks a carrier at checkout, finance wants to A/B test a flat rate, and a new carrier arrives every quarter. Each rule becomes a `ShippingQuote` strategy with its own unit tests, and the checkout service stays unchanged.

ShippingQuote chosen = flags.on("flat-shipping", user) ? flat : dhl;

blocks.text: Payoff: a new carrier is a new class plus one registry line. The flat-rate experiment is one lambda behind a flag.

lists.title: Use when
items: Several variants of one algorithm must be swappable at runtime.
A growing `switch` on a type or code picks behaviour.
You want each rule unit-tested in isolation.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: There are two variants that will never change: an `if` is clearer.
Variants need different inputs, so one interface cannot fit them all.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Context checking `instanceof` on its strategy, which defeats the pattern.
Clients must now know every strategy; hide the choice behind a registry or factory.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: An interface plus classes for a rule that a lambda would cover.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Functional interfaces and lambdas replace most strategy class hierarchies.
For a closed set of data-driven rules, a sealed interface plus `switch` pattern matching can be simpler.

rows.difference: Same shape, different intent. With State the object switches its own state as events arrive and the states know each other. With Strategy the client chooses and strategies are independent.
Template Method varies steps through inheritance, fixed at compile time. Strategy varies the whole algorithm through composition, at runtime.
A command packages a request to run, queue or undo later. A strategy answers *how* to do one job right now.
Decorator changes an object's behaviour by wrapping it from the outside; Strategy replaces its internals.
A factory or registry often picks the strategy from configuration, and DI injects it.

options.why: The job delegates one varying algorithm (encoding) to an injected, interchangeable `Codec`.
Nothing transitions: the codec is fixed for the job's life and never replaces itself.
There is no second abstraction hierarchy being developed independently; it is one job with one pluggable step.
There is no abstract superclass with overridable steps; the variation comes through composition.

template: interface Codec { String extension(); byte[] encode(byte[] raw); }

exercises.scenario: A tax engine computes VAT differently per country. The rule is chosen at checkout from the shipping address, new countries are added monthly, and a rule never changes during one calculation.

options.why: One varying algorithm, selected from outside per request, with new variants added without touching the engine.
There is no lifecycle and no transitions; the rule does not change itself as events arrive.
A subclass per country fixes the choice at compile time and couples every rule to one base-class skeleton.
The responsible rule is known up front from the address; there is nothing to pass along a chain.

exercises.prompt: Explain Strategy in your own words: what varies, who chooses, and how it differs from State.

modelAnswer.text: Strategy pulls one varying algorithm out of a class behind an interface. The context delegates to whatever strategy it was given, and the client or configuration chooses it, usually at construction. Unlike State, strategies don't know each other and the context doesn't swap them in response to its own events.

keyPoints: One varying algorithm behind one interface
Context delegates and never inspects the concrete type
The client or config chooses, often by injection
State changes itself and knows the transitions; Strategy is chosen from outside
In modern Java a lambda can be the strategy
